label: Nara-ehon
defn: Illustrated books and scrolls of tales painted in bright mineral colours by largely anonymous town painters of Kyoto, late 16th–18th century: Tales of Ise, Bunshō zōshi, otogi-zōshi booklets.
note: Nara-ehon redirects to E-hon; anonymous workshop tradition, so built here rather than in the artist pass

label: Ōtsu-e
defn: Folk paintings sold to travellers at Ōtsu on the Tōkaidō from the 17th century, brushed quickly with stencils and few colours: the Demon Chanting the Nembutsu, Wisteria Maiden, Fujimusume, Buddhist icons.

label: Ema
defn: Painted wooden votive plaques offered at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples, from small mass-made tablets to large framed ema halls painted by town and ukiyo-e painters: horse ema, Kitano Tenmangū votive tablets.
note: named painters (Hokusai, Kuniyoshi) are see-also to the artist pass

label: Minhwa
defn: Korean folk painting of the late Joseon period, anonymous decorative screens and scrolls for houses: chaekgeori book-and-scholar's-object screens, munjado ideograph paintings, magpie and tiger, sipjangsaeng ten longevity symbols.
note: court chaekgeori (Yi Eung-rok) belongs to the artist pass; folk chaekgeori is a kind here

label: Nianhua
defn: Chinese New Year pictures: popular colour woodblock prints of door gods, auspicious children and opera scenes pasted up at the New Year, made in named print towns: Yangliuqing, Taohuawu, Yangjiabu, Zhuxianzhen.
aliases: New Year picture;Chinese New Year prints;nianhua woodblock prints
note: print towns are kinds (P7: the field names the prints after them)

label: Dunhuang Manuscripts
defn: The manuscripts sealed in the Library Cave (Cave 17) of the Mogao Caves about 1000 and opened in 1900: Buddhist sutras, documents and the earliest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra of 868, with illustrated sutra frontispieces.

label: Uigwe
defn: Illustrated royal protocol books of the Joseon court (1392–1910), recording ceremonies, weddings and funerals in text and painted processions: Hwaseong seongyeok uigwe, Banchado procession paintings.

label: Sutra Copying
defn: Buddhist sutras transcribed as acts of devotion and decorated with gold and silver on dyed paper, frontispiece paintings and ornamented rollers in Japan and Korea: the Heike Nōkyō, Lotus Sutra fan papers, Goryeo sagyeong in gold on indigo paper.
note: Korean Goryeo sutras are a kind; seam with Chinese painting of sutra frontispieces

label: Dongba Manuscripts
defn: Ritual manuscripts of the Naxi Dongba priests of Lijiang in Yunnan, written in pictographic Dongba script and painted with deities, with painted ritual cards and scrolls.
note: UNESCO Memory of the World (2003); Dongba scroll paintings kept as a kind of the manuscript tradition

label: Chinese Paper Cutting
defn: Designs cut from red and coloured paper with scissors or knives for windows, doors and festivals across China (UNESCO 2009): window flowers (chuanghua), xi double-happiness cuts, embroidery patterns.

label: Netsuke
defn: Miniature toggles carved in ivory, wood and other materials to secure hanging containers to the kimono sash, Edo to Meiji period, with named carvers and regional schools: katabori figures, manjū netsuke, sashi netsuke.
note: wood netsuke also sit here: the carving tradition, not the material, is the leaf

label: Chinese Jade
defn: Nephrite and later jadeite carved in China from the Neolithic to the Qing: ritual bi discs and cong tubes of Hongshan and Liangzhu, Shang and Zhou pendants and Han burial suits, Qing imperial boulders and vessels.

label: Chinese Snuff Bottles
defn: Small stoppered bottles made at the Qing court and in China's workshops (late 17th–20th century) in hardstone, glass, porcelain, enamel and lacquer, including inside-painted glass: Beijing palace glass bottles, carved agate, inside-painted bottles.
note: an object type the field treats as a collecting tradition (cf. G1-8); multi-material, placed in D3 for its hardstone core

label: Chinese Shadow Puppetry
defn: Translucent puppets cut from leather or paper and painted, used in shadow theatre across China (UNESCO 2011), with regional styles: Shaanxi, Tangshan (Luanzhou), Sichuan puppets.

label: Bunraku
defn: The puppets of the Japanese ningyō jōruri theatre, carved and painted wooden heads (kashira) with mechanisms and costumed bodies worked by three puppeteers, and regional puppet troupes.
note: leaf is the puppet as an object; the performance itself is outside Visual Art

label: Korean Masks
defn: Carved wooden and gourd masks of Korean mask-dance drama (talchum) and village rites, by regional tradition: Hahoe and Byeongsan masks (National Treasure), Bongsan, Yangju, Ogwangdae masks.
note: each regional mask-dance drama with its own mask set is a kind

label: Haniwa
defn: Unglazed terracotta cylinders and figures set on and around Kofun-period burial mounds in Japan (3rd–6th century): warriors in armour, horses, houses, dancing figures.
note: clay figure as image → D before E (tab key 7)

label: Mingqi
defn: Figures and models made to furnish Chinese tombs, from Han pottery houses and attendants to Tang lead-glazed camels, horses and tomb guardians: sancai camel with musicians, zhenmushou tomb guardians, Northern Wei soldiers.
aliases: Chinese tomb figures;tomb pottery;Tang dynasty tomb figures
note: sancai-glazed vessels go to Tang Sancai; figures stay here

label: Chinese Buddhist Sculpture
defn: Buddhist images in China in stone, bronze, wood and clay from the 4th century, in cave temples and for altars: Yungang and Longmen caves, Xiangtangshan reliefs, Liao painted wooden Guanyin, Dazu rock carvings.
note: rock-cut and cave sculpture is kept here rather than in L (it is carving, not painting or rock art)

label: Korean Buddhist Sculpture
defn: Buddhist images of the Three Kingdoms, Unified Silla, Goryeo and Joseon in gilt bronze, stone and wood: pensive bodhisattvas, Seokguram, the Seosan rock-carved triad.

label: Japanese Buddhist Sculpture
defn: Buddhist images of Japan in bronze, lacquer and wood from the Asuka period onward, made by workshop lineages of sculptors (busshi): Tori school Shaka triad, Tōdai-ji guardian kings, Kei school Kamakura figures.
note: redirect from Japanese Buddhist sculpture; workshop lineages (Kei, In, En) are kinds for the artist pass

label: Japanese Dolls (Ningyō)
defn: Japanese dolls and folk toys of clay, wood, papier-mâché and fabric, made in named regional centres: Hakata and Fushimi clay dolls, Kyō-ningyō, hina dolls, inu-hariko papier-mâché dogs.

label: Kokeshi
defn: Lathe-turned and painted wooden dolls of the Tōhoku hot-spring towns (from the 19th century), in named lineages: Naruko, Tōgatta, Tsuchiyu kokeshi.

label: Huishan Clay Figurines
defn: Painted clay figurines from Huishan near Wuxi in Jiangsu (Ming to the present): A-fu plump children, opera figures (shouniezi).

label: Clay Figure Zhang
defn: The painted clay figure sculpture of the Zhang family workshop of Tianjin, founded by Zhang Mingshan (1826–1906): genre figures and opera characters modelled with realism.

label: Tu'er Ye
defn: Clay figures of the Moon Rabbit dressed as a warrior or official, made in Beijing for the Mid-Autumn Festival since the Ming.

label: Yangshao Painted Pottery
defn: Hand-built red earthenware painted in black and red of the Neolithic Yellow River cultures (c. 5000–2000 BCE): Banpo fish-and-face basins, Miaodigou bowls, Majiayao and Banshan spiral jars of Gansu.
aliases: Neolithic Chinese painted pottery;Majiayao pottery;Gansu painted pottery
note: P13: archaeological culture known for its pottery

label: Jōmon Pottery
defn: Cord-marked earthenware of the Jōmon hunter-gatherers of Japan (c. 14,000–300 BCE), among the oldest pottery in the world: flame-style (kaen) vessels, deep cord-marked jars, and clay dogū figurines.
note: dogū kept as a kind (P13)

label: Yayoi Pottery
defn: Wheel-finished, smooth reddish earthenware of the Yayoi period in Japan (c. 300 BCE–300 CE): storage jars, pedestalled bowls and cooking pots, first found at Yayoi in Tokyo.

label: Tang Sancai
defn: Lead-glazed earthenware splashed in amber, green and cream (and rarely cobalt) made in Tang China for tombs and for use: phoenix-head ewers, dishes with stamped designs, camels and horses, and its Liao and Song successors.
note: Tang sancai figures are Mingqi; vessels here

label: Raku Ware
defn: Hand-modelled, low-fired tea bowls made in Kyoto from the 1570s by Chōjirō and the Raku family for the wabi tea ceremony: black Raku and red Raku bowls, and Hon'ami Kōetsu's bowls.
note: no pool row names it: built from the Momoyama period row (ceramics 90)

label: Satsuma Ware
defn: Pottery of Satsuma province in southern Kyushu founded by Korean potters (from 1598), from dark stoneware (kuro-satsuma) to the crackled ivory earthenware painted in enamels and gold for export in the Meiji era (Kyō-Satsuma, Yokohama-Satsuma).
note: kuro-satsuma is stoneware: placed in E1 by its best-known export body

label: Onggi
defn: Korean earthenware storage jars glazed with wood-ash and leaf-mould glaze, coil-built and paddled for fermenting kimchi, soy and pastes; master potters designated onggijang.

label: Yue Ware
defn: Grey-green celadon stoneware of Zhejiang (Eastern Han to Song), centred on Shanglin Lake, the first great Chinese celadon: chicken-head ewers, Five Dynasties mise (secret colour) ware made for the Wuyue court.

label: Yaozhou Ware
defn: Northern celadon of Tongchuan in Shaanxi (Tang to Yuan), olive-green glaze over crisply carved and moulded peonies and waves.

label: Longquan Celadon
defn: Celadon stoneware of the Longquan kilns in southern Zhejiang (Song to Ming), in thick bluish-green glazes and exported across Asia (UNESCO 2009): kinuta vases, mallet vases, large Ming dishes.

label: Ru Ware
defn: The rare celadon made for the Northern Song court at Qingliangsi in Henan (c. 1086–1125), with a crackled duck-egg-blue glaze; fewer than a hundred pieces survive.
note: kiln evidence: excluded row Ru (workshop, kilns)

label: Guan Ware
defn: Official ware of the Southern Song court at Hangzhou (Xiuneisi and Jiaotanxia kilns), thin dark-bodied stoneware with thick crackled glaze.

label: Jun Ware
defn: Stoneware of Henan (Song to Yuan) with an opalescent lavender-blue glaze splashed with copper purple: flowerpots and stands, bowls and dishes.

label: Jian Ware
defn: Dark-glazed tea bowls of Jianyang in Fujian (Song), prized in Japan as tenmoku: hare's fur, oil-spot and yōhen bowls.

label: Cizhou Ware
defn: Popular stoneware of northern China (Song to Ming) decorated through white slip by sgraffito, carving and black painting: pillows, meiping vases, jars painted with fish and peonies.
note: built from the Jin dynasty row (ceramics 76)

label: Yixing Ware
defn: Unglazed purple-clay (zisha) stoneware of Yixing in Jiangsu (from the 16th century), above all small teapots by named potters such as Gong Chun and Shi Dabin.
note: no pool row; named in the slice instructions

label: Goryeo Celadon
defn: The celadon stoneware of Goryeo Korea (10th–14th century) from the kilns of Gangjin and Buan, with jade-green glaze and inlaid (sanggam) decoration: maebyeong vases, kundika, incense burners.
note: built from the Goryeo dynasty row (ceramics 160) and the Korean row (ceramics 318)

label: Buncheong
defn: Grey stoneware of early Joseon Korea (15th–16th century) covered in white slip that is stamped, inlaid, incised, painted or brushed: mishima, hakeme and kohiki bowls prized in Japan.
note: built from the Joseon dynasty row (ceramics 78)

label: Seto Ware
defn: Glazed stoneware of Seto in Owari, Japan's only glazed medieval kiln (from the 13th century), imitating Chinese celadon and tenmoku, and the tea wares of the neighbouring Mino kilns in the Momoyama period: Ko-Seto jars, Ki-Seto, Setoguro bowls.
note: Mino ware (Q11609247) is the Mino side of this tradition; its named wares Shino and Oribe are leaves

label: Shino Ware
defn: Momoyama-period tea ware of the Mino kilns with a thick, pitted white feldspar glaze, sometimes painted in iron: e-Shino, nezumi (grey) Shino, the Unohanagaki tea bowl.

label: Oribe Ware
defn: Mino stoneware of the early 17th century named for the tea master Furuta Oribe, with copper-green glaze and boldly painted iron designs in asymmetric forms: kutsu (clog) tea bowls, fan-shaped dishes.

label: Bizen Ware
defn: Unglazed, wood-fired stoneware of Imbe in Okayama, one of the Six Ancient Kilns, with fire-marks (hidasuki, goma): tea-ceremony water jars, hanaire flower vases.

label: Shigaraki Ware
defn: Wood-fired stoneware of Shigaraki in Shiga, one of the Six Ancient Kilns, with feldspar inclusions and natural ash glaze: storage jars and tea wares.

label: Iga Ware
defn: Wood-fired stoneware of Iga in Mie, close to Shigaraki, with heavy ash glaze and distorted forms favoured for Momoyama tea vases and water jars.

label: Tamba Ware
defn: Stoneware of Tachikui in Hyōgo, one of the Six Ancient Kilns: ash-glazed storage jars and, from the Edo period, slip and glaze wares.

label: Tokoname Ware
defn: Stoneware of the Chita peninsula in Aichi, the largest of the Six Ancient Kilns: large medieval storage jars and later red-clay teapots.

label: Echizen Ware
defn: Stoneware of Fukui, one of the Six Ancient Kilns, descended from Tokoname techniques: ash-glazed storage jars and mortars.

label: Karatsu Ware
defn: Stoneware of northern Kyushu begun by Korean potters in the late 16th century, iron-painted (e-Garatsu) and glaze-patterned for tea and daily use.

label: Hagi Ware
defn: Soft stoneware of Hagi in Yamaguchi founded by Korean potters (1604), with pale crackled glazes that change with use, chiefly tea bowls.

label: Takatori Ware
defn: Stoneware of Fukuoka founded by the Korean potter Hachizō (early 17th century), refined tea caddies and bowls with flowing glazes for the Enshū taste.

label: Agano Ware
defn: Stoneware of Fukuchi in Fukuoka founded by Korean potters in the early 17th century, with green copper and iron glazes; one of Kobori Enshū's seven kilns.

label: Kyō Ware
defn: The pottery of Kyoto from the 17th century, overglaze-enamelled and painterly, by named potters and kilns: Nonomura Ninsei's enamelled tea jars, Ogata Kenzan's painted dishes, Awata and Kiyomizu wares.
note: Ninsei and Kenzan are named-maker kinds for the artist pass

label: Onta Ware
defn: Folk stoneware of a hamlet in Hita, Ōita, made by a few families since 1705 with slip, combed (tobiganna) and poured decoration; championed by the Mingei movement.

label: Koishiwara Ware
defn: Folk stoneware of Tōhō, Fukuoka (from the 17th century), the parent kiln of Onta, decorated with chattering (tobiganna) and brushed slip.

label: Mumyōi Ware
defn: High-fired red stoneware of Sado island made from iron-rich mumyōi clay, burnished and fired to a deep red-to-black (from the 19th century).

label: Ding Ware
defn: Thin ivory-white porcelain of Quyang in Hebei (Tang to Yuan), fired upside-down with unglazed rims bound in metal, with carved and moulded lotus designs.

label: Xing Ware
defn: White porcelain of Hebei (Tang), the first fine Chinese white ware, paired in Tang texts with Yue celadon.
note: attested by an excluded pool row

label: Qingbai Ware
defn: Bluish-white porcelain of Jingdezhen and southern China (Song and Yuan), translucent with a pale blue glaze pooling in carved designs.

label: Chinese Blue-and-White Porcelain
defn: Porcelain painted in cobalt under the glaze, made at Jingdezhen from the Yuan dynasty: Yuan large dishes, Ming imperial Xuande and Chenghua wares, Transitional and Kangxi porcelain.
note: article opens with the Jingdezhen tradition

label: Doucai
defn: 'Contending colours': underglaze-blue outlines filled with overglaze enamels, perfected at Jingdezhen under the Chenghua emperor (1465–87): chicken cups, Yongzheng doucai dishes.

label: Wucai
defn: 'Five-colour' porcelain of Jingdezhen (Jiajing and Wanli reigns) combining underglaze blue with red, green and yellow overglaze enamels, the precursor of famille verte.

label: Famille Verte
defn: Kangxi-period (1662–1722) Jingdezhen porcelain painted in overglaze enamels dominated by greens, with yellow-ground (famille jaune) and black-ground (famille noire) variants.
note: the combined Wikipedia article Familles jaune, noire, rose, and verte covers both palettes

label: Famille Rose
defn: Porcelain painted in opaque pink and other overglaze enamels developed from European enamel in the 1720s: falangcai palace wares, yangcai, and export Rose Medallion and Rose Mandarin.

label: Jingdezhen Porcelain
defn: The porcelain of Jingdezhen's imperial and private kilns other than its named decorative wares: monochromes (peachbloom, robin's-egg, tea-dust), anhua hidden decoration, underglaze red and the imperial reign-marked wares of the Ming and Qing.
note: residual leaf on the pilot pattern (cf. E2-10)

label: Kraak Ware
defn: Thin Jingdezhen blue-and-white export porcelain of the Wanli reign and after (c. 1570–1650), with panelled borders, shipped in quantity by the Portuguese and Dutch.

label: Swatow Ware
defn: Coarse export porcelain of the Zhangzhou kilns in Fujian (late 16th–17th century), blue-and-white and enamelled, traded to Southeast Asia and Japan.
note: evidence: excluded rows Chinese, Shantou (36) and Chinese, Swatow (8)

label: Chinese Export Porcelain
defn: Porcelain made in China for European and American markets (16th–19th century) to order or in export styles: armorial services, Jesuit ware, Canton famille rose (Rose Medallion), Chine de commande.
note: Met "Chinese, Export" row (ceramics 613) attests it; its textiles are tagged

label: Dehua Porcelain
defn: White porcelain of Dehua in Fujian (Ming and Qing), with an ivory glaze, known in Europe as blanc de Chine: Guanyin figures by He Chaozong, libation cups.

label: Joseon White Porcelain
defn: The white porcelain (baekja) of the Joseon court kilns at Gwangju (15th–19th century), plain or painted in underglaze cobalt, iron and copper: moon jars, blue-and-white dragon jars.
note: built from the Joseon dynasty row (ceramics 78)

label: Arita Ware
defn: Porcelain of Arita in Hizen (Kyushu) from about 1616, shipped from Imari: shoki-Imari blue-and-white, Ko-Imari gold-and-red export ware, Dutch East India Company commissions.
note: Kakiemon and Nabeshima kept as leaves (separately named wares); Imari is a kind

label: Kakiemon
defn: Arita porcelain enamelled in the style of the Sakaida Kakiemon family (from the 1640s), sparse asymmetric designs on a milk-white body (nigoshide), copied at Meissen and Chantilly.

label: Nabeshima Ware
defn: Porcelain of the Nabeshima clan kiln at Ōkawachi (late 17th–19th century), made for gifts to the shogun: footed dishes with underglaze blue and enamel designs.

label: Hirado Ware
defn: Fine white porcelain of Mikawachi near Hirado (18th–19th century), painted in soft blue and finely modelled, often with Chinese boys under pines.

label: Kutani Ware
defn: Overglaze-enamelled porcelain associated with Kutani in Kaga: Ko-Kutani (17th century) in bold green, yellow and purple, and the 19th-century revival kilns (Yoshidaya, Eiraku).

label: Chinese Ritual Bronzes
defn: Bronze vessels and bells cast in piece-moulds for ancestral rites from the Erligang and Shang to the Han: ding cauldrons, gu and jue wine vessels, taotie masks, inscribed Western Zhou gui.
note: built from the Shang, Zhou and Western Zhou period rows

label: Ordos Bronzes
defn: Cast bronze belt plaques, knives and fittings in the steppe animal style from the Ordos and northern frontier of China (6th–1st century BCE).
note: built from the North China (metalwork 87) row; seam with the ancient_world steppe rows

label: Yugi
defn: Korean bronze tableware forged or cast from high-tin bronze (bangjja yugi), of Anseong and Napcheong; makers designated yugijang.
note: attested by the pool row Yugijang (brassware making)

label: Ipsa
defn: Korean inlay of silver and gold wire into iron and bronze (Goryeo to Joseon): incense burners, kundika and furniture fittings; makers designated ipsajang.
note: attested by the pool row Ipsajang (silver or gold inlaying)

label: Japanese Swords
defn: Blades forged and polished by Japanese swordsmiths in named traditions and schools: tachi, katana, tantō of the five traditions (Yamashiro, Yamato, Bizen, Sōshū, Mino).

label: Japanese Sword Mountings
defn: Metal sword fittings (tosogu) made by schools of metalworkers from the Muromachi to the Meiji: tsuba guards, menuki, kozuka, fuchi-kashira, in shakudō, shibuichi and mokume-gane.
note: Met classification sword furniture (2958) is the evidence; schools (Gotō, Higo) are kinds

label: Miao Silver Ornaments
defn: Silver headdresses, neck-rings and breastplates hammered and filigreed by Miao smiths of Guizhou for festival dress.
note: museum page (Bowers Museum, Miao Masters of Silver); no Wikipedia article

label: Jangdo
defn: Korean ornamental knives in silver, horn and wood worn on the hanbok as accessory and symbol of fidelity; makers designated jangdojang.
note: attested by the pool row Jangdojang

label: Kesi
defn: Silk tapestry woven with discontinuous wefts in China from the Tang, reproducing paintings and calligraphy in the Song and dressing the Qing court: Shen Zifan's kesi landscapes, dragon robes.
note: QID of the excluded pool row k'o-ssu; built from the Chinese (textiles 1940) and Qing (textiles 1259) rows

label: Zhuang Brocade
defn: Weft-patterned cotton-and-silk brocade of the Zhuang of Guangxi, one of China's four famous brocades.

label: Li Textiles
defn: The spinning, ikat-dyeing, weaving and embroidery of the Li (Hlai) women of Hainan (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2009): tube skirts, dragon quilts.

label: Shuri Weaving
defn: The court textiles of Shuri, the Ryukyu capital: hanaori and rōton-ori figured weaves and kasuri silks.

label: Bashōfu
defn: Cloth woven from Japanese banana fibre in Okinawa and Amami, plain or kasuri-patterned, centred on Kijoka.

label: Echigo-jōfu and Ojiya-chijimi
defn: Fine ramie cloth of the Uonuma region of Niigata, snow-bleached and often kasuri-patterned (UNESCO 2009).

label: Hansan Mosi
defn: Fine ramie cloth woven by women of Hansan in South Chungcheong (UNESCO 2011), for summer hanbok.

label: Suzhou Embroidery
defn: Silk embroidery of Suzhou in Jiangsu, one of China's four famous embroideries, fine-split thread and double-sided pieces: cats, goldfish, painting copies.

label: Xiang Embroidery
defn: Silk embroidery of Changsha in Hunan, one of the four famous embroideries, famed for tigers and lions in shaded stitches.

label: Shu Embroidery
defn: Silk embroidery of Chengdu in Sichuan, one of the four famous embroideries: pandas, carp and hibiscus on satin.

label: Cantonese Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of the Pearl River Delta (Guangzhou and Chaozhou), dense and brilliant, with raised gold-thread work; one of the four famous embroideries.
note: Chaozhou (Chaoshan) embroidery is a kind

label: Gu Embroidery
defn: Painting-embroidery of the Gu family of Shanghai (late Ming), copying Song and Yuan paintings in silk thread: Han Ximeng's albums.

label: Korean Embroidery
defn: Silk embroidery of Joseon court and household (jasu): embroidered screens, rank badges (hyungbae), pillow ends, wedding robes (hwarot); masters designated jasujang.

label: Bojagi
defn: Korean wrapping cloths, above all jogakbo patchwork of leftover ramie and silk, and embroidered subo.

label: Sashiko
defn: Japanese running-stitch quilting and darning of indigo cloth, in regional forms: kogin of Tsugaru, hishizashi, mended boro.

label: Hmong Textile Art
defn: Embroidery, batik, appliqué and pleating of the Miao (Hmong) of Guizhou and the Hmong diaspora: pleated skirts, baby carriers, story cloths (paj ntaub).
note: seam with southeast_asia (Hmong of Laos and Thailand)

label: Ainu Textiles
defn: Ainu robes of elm-bark (attus) and nettle cloth and of imported cotton, with appliqué and chain-stitch embroidery of curving designs: ruunpe, chikarkarpe, kaparamip.

label: Yūzen
defn: Paste-resist dyeing with a fine rice-paste line and painted dyes, attributed to Miyazaki Yūzensai of Kyoto (late 17th century): Kyō-yūzen and Kaga-yūzen kimono.
note: built from the Japanese (textiles 4215) and Edo (textiles 1593) rows

label: Katazome
defn: Japanese stencil dyeing with paste applied through cut paper stencils (katagami), and the stencils themselves as collected objects: Ise-katagami, komon small-pattern kimono.
note: katagami (1824 objects) are the evidence; seam with C4 paper arts

label: Bingata
defn: Okinawan stencil- and freehand paste-resist cloth dyed in bright pigments, made for the Ryukyu court and gentry.

label: Tsutsugaki
defn: Freehand paste-resist dyeing with a cone (tsutsu), mostly indigo, for festive covers, futon covers and banners (Edo to early 20th century).

label: Shibori
defn: Japanese shaped-resist dyeing by binding, stitching, folding and capping cloth: kanoko dots, arimatsu-narumi shibori, the Momoyama tsujigahana robes.

label: Kasuri
defn: Japanese ikat: cotton, ramie and silk cloth woven from resist-dyed threads, in regional centres: Kurume, Iyo, Bingo, Miyako-jōfu.

label: Bai Tie-Dye
defn: Indigo tie-dyed cotton (zharan) of the Bai of Dali and Zhoucheng in Yunnan.
note: encyclopedia entry (national ICH 2006); no Wikipedia article

label: Geumbak
defn: Korean gold-leaf stamping of textiles with carved woodblocks, for royal and bridal dress; makers designated geumbakjang.

label: Kumihimo
defn: Japanese braided silk cords made on stands (marudai, takadai), for sword mounts, armour lacing and obijime.

label: Maedeup
defn: Korean decorative knotting in silk cord, with tassels for norigae pendants and ritual objects; makers designated maedeupjang.

label: Chaesang
defn: Korean boxes of dyed bamboo strips woven in patterns; makers designated chaesangjang.

label: Wanchojang
defn: Korean weaving of sedge (wanchoe) into patterned mats (hwamunseok), baskets and cushions, especially of Ganghwa island.
note: label is the craft designation; see problems

label: Yosegi-zaiku
defn: Wood mosaic of Hakone: blocks of differently coloured woods glued into patterns and planed into veneers for boxes and puzzle boxes.

label: Ainu Woodcarving
defn: Ainu carving of wood in curving and scale designs: prayer sticks (ikupasuy), trays, knife hilts (makiri) and ritual objects, and the carved trays of Nibutani.
note: attest names the defining object type; see problems

label: Hwagak
defn: Korean painted ox-horn veneer: thin translucent horn sheets painted on the back in bright colours and laid on boxes and furniture; makers designated hwagakjang.

label: Carved Lacquer
defn: Chinese lacquer built up in many layers and carved in relief, from the Song: tihong cinnabar lacquer, tixi guri scrolls, Yongle and Qianlong imperial boxes.

label: Maki-e
defn: Japanese lacquer decorated with sprinkled gold and silver powder, from the Heian period: Kōdaiji maki-e, Hon'ami Kōetsu's writing boxes, inrō, Nanban export lacquer.

label: Japanese Lacquerware
defn: Japanese lacquer other than maki-e, made in regional centres named for their wares: Wajima-nuri, Tsugaru-nuri, Kamakura-bori, Negoro, and raden mother-of-pearl inlay.
note: residual leaf on the pilot pattern

label: Ryukyuan Lacquerware
defn: Lacquer of the Ryukyu kingdom (15th–19th century) with red grounds, mother-of-pearl inlay, gold-leaf (chinkin) and relief (tsuikin) decoration.
note: Met "Japanese, Ryūkyū Islands" lacquer 25 is evidence

label: Najeonchilgi
defn: Korean lacquer inlaid with mother-of-pearl, from Goryeo sutra boxes to Joseon clothing chests; makers designated najeonjang and chiljang.

label: Yi Lacquerware
defn: Red, yellow and black painted lacquer of the Yi (Nuosu) of Liangshan in Sichuan: wooden bowls, cups and armour.
note: scholarly article on Liangshan Yi lacquerware (national ICH); no Wikipedia article

label: Kintsugi
defn: Japanese repair of broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with gold, valued as an aesthetic in its own right since the 16th century.

label: Soban
defn: Korean small portable dining tables of wood in regional styles (Naju, Haeju, Tongyeong); makers designated sobanjang.

label: Zuojiang Huashan Rock Art
defn: Red-ochre rock paintings of the Luo Yue people on cliffs along the Zuojiang river in Guangxi (5th c. BCE–2nd c. CE), with figures and bronze drums (UNESCO 2016).

label: Bangudae Petroglyphs
defn: Neolithic and Bronze Age petroglyphs on the Daegok stream in Ulsan, with whales, hunters and boats, and the nearby Cheonjeon-ri carvings (UNESCO 2025).

label: Fugoppe Cave
defn: Incised figures and signs in the Fugoppe cave in Hokkaido (Epi-Jōmon) and the related Temiya cave carvings.

label: Helan Mountains Petroglyphs
defn: Petroglyphs pecked on the cliffs of the Helan and Yin mountains of Ningxia and Inner Mongolia, from the Neolithic to the medieval period: masks, animals and hunters (Helankou, Damaidi).
note: see problems: no standalone article

label: Dunhuang Murals
defn: The wall paintings of the Buddhist cave temples of Dunhuang (4th–14th century), in the Mogao and Yulin caves: Jataka tales, Pure Land paradise scenes, donor portraits.

label: Yongle Palace Murals
defn: The Daoist murals of the Yongle Palace in Shanxi (14th century), with the procession of deities in the Hall of Three Purities, and the Buddhist murals of the Fahai Temple near Beijing (1443).

label: Takamatsuzuka Tomb Murals
defn: Painted plaster walls of the late 7th-century tombs of Asuka (Takamatsuzuka and Kitora), with court ladies, the Four Directional Animals and star charts.
note: Hōryū-ji Golden Hall murals kept as a kind (same period, Buddhist)

label: Goguryeo Tomb Murals
defn: The wall paintings of the Goguryeo tombs near Pyongyang and Ji'an (4th–7th century): hunting scenes, dancers and the Four Guardians (UNESCO 2004).

label: Dancheong
defn: Korean polychrome painting of wooden buildings, temples and palaces in blue, red, yellow, white and black patterns; masters designated dancheongjang.

label: Gozan no Okuribi
defn: The five bonfire characters and figures (Daimonji, Myōhō, the boat and the torii) lit on the hills around Kyoto on 16 August, laid out as fixed hillside figures.
note: an ephemeral fire-geoglyph; see problems

label: Irezumi
defn: Japanese tattooing, above all the Edo-period full-body designs inspired by ukiyo-e heroes, with the Okinawan women's hand tattoos (hajichi) and Ainu lip tattoos as kinds.
